claim: Only a small portion of BRM is bound to chromatin at any given time, with approximately 95% residing in the nucleoplasm.
source: Co-localization analysis of BRM and DAPI yielded a Manders coefficient of 0.05, implying that only a small proportion of BRM is chromatin engaged at any given moment.
evidence: The Manders coefficient of 0.05 from co-localization analysis provides quantitative data supporting this claim.

claim: BRM preferentially associates with decondensed chromatin in interbands and is excluded from highly compacted bands.
source: A line-scan illustrates the preferential association of BRM with decondensed chromatin and its exclusion from highly compacted bands (Figure 1C).
evidence: Line-scan analysis and immunofluorescence imaging provide direct observational data.

claim: BRM binds to loci within interbands and puffs on polytene chromosomes.
source: In agreement with early studies (Armstrong et al., 2002; Mohrmann et al., 2004), visualization of endogenous BRM on fixated polytene chromosome spreads by epi-immunofluorescence (IF) revealed binding to loci within interbands, and to puffs (Figure 1A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data and citations to previous studies support this claim.

claim: BRM is largely excluded from heterochromatic bands.
source: BRM is largely excluded from heterochromatic bands, which stain strongly with DAPI and with antibodies directed against the core histones (α-HIS).
evidence: Immunofluorescence observations provide direct evidence.

claim: Depletion of BRM does not lead to gross changes in the polytene chromosome banding pattern or the binding of RNAPII.
source: Depletion of BRM affects does not lead to gross changes in the polytene chromosome banding pattern or the binding of RNAPII (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence analysis after RNAi-mediated depletion provides experimental evidence.

claim: The majority of RNAPII is associated with well-defined chromosomal loci and has lower abundance in the nucleoplasm compared to BRM.
source: For comparison, the majority of RNAPII associated with well-defined chromosomal loci and has a lower abundance in the nucleoplasm (Figure 1D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging provides comparative data.

claim: GFP-BRM is efficiently incorporated into remodeler complexes.
source: MOR (SMARCC1/2) co-immunopurifications (co-IPs) from dissected larval salivary gland extracts revealed the efficient incorporation of GFP-BRM in remodeler complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments provide biochemical evidence.

claim: GFP-BRM binds chromatin normally as part of (P)BAP complexes.
source: IF of polytene chromosomes showed extensive co-localization of GFP-BRM with endogenous MOR, confirming that it binds chromatin normally as part of (P)BAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence co-localization provides direct evidence.

claim: GFP-BRM predominantly exists as part of (P)BAP complexes.
source: RNAi-mediated depletion of MOR in the larval salivary gland caused a concomitant loss of GFP-BRM, indicating that it predominantly exists as part of (P)BAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: RNAi depletion experiments provide functional evidence.

claim: MOR has a key architectural function that is essential for the structural integrity of (P)BAP and the stability of BRM in vivo.
source: MOR has a key architectural function that is essential for the structural integrity of (P)BAP and the stability of BRM in vivo (Moshkin et al., 2007).
evidence: Citation to previous study supports this claim.

claim: The volume of polytene chromosomes in nuclear space comprises approximately 5% black, 43% gray, and 52% white chromatin.
source: This analysis indicated that the volume of polytene chromosomes in nuclear space comprises about 5 (±1) % black, 43 (±4) % gray, and 52 (±5) % white chromatin (Figure 1H).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of GFP-H2B intensity distribution provides measurement data.

claim: Chromatin in gray bands is on average sixfold more condensed than in interbands.
source: Applying these estimates of GFP-H2B density distribution in living cells implies that chromatin in gray bands is on average sixfold more condensed than in interbands, whereas black chromatin is condensed an additional ~25-fold (up to ~150 more than open chromatin).
evidence: Calculation based on GFP-H2B density measurements provides quantitative evidence.

claim: Black chromatin is condensed up to approximately 150-fold more than open chromatin.
source: Applying these estimates of GFP-H2B density distribution in living cells implies that chromatin in gray bands is on average sixfold more condensed than in interbands, whereas black chromatin is condensed an additional ~25-fold (up to ~150 more than open chromatin).
evidence: Calculation based on GFP-H2B density measurements provides quantitative evidence.

claim: Both BAP and PBAP bind the repressed E74 and E75 loci before Ec induction.
source: Before induction, both OSA and PBRM were present at E74 and E75.
evidence: Immunofluorescence observations provide direct evidence.

claim: Only PBAP, but not BAP, is recruited to E74 and E75 loci after transcriptional activation by Ec.
source: After puffing, PBRM accumulated on the E74 and E75 loci, but we detected no appreciable binding of OSA (Figure 2D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging after Ec treatment provides direct observational evidence.

claim: PBRM co-localizes with EcR on the E74 and E75 loci.
source: On the E74 and E75 loci, PBRM co-localized with the EcR (Figure 2E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence co-localization provides direct evidence.

claim: PBAP is required for Ec-controlled gene regulation in vivo.
source: Loss of BAP170 (ARID2) and PBRM disrupted the expression of the E74 and E75 genes, showing that PBAP is required for Ec-controlled gene regulation in vivo.
evidence: RT-qPCR analysis of mutant prepupae provides functional evidence.

claim: Loss of PBAP signature subunits, but not OSA, abrogates E74 and E75 gene induction by Ec in S2 cells.
source: Again, the loss of PBAP signature subunits, but not OSA, abrogated gene induction by Ec.
evidence: RT-qPCR analysis after RNAi depletion in S2 cells provides experimental evidence.

claim: The EcR binding sites within the E74 and E75 loci cover approximately 40 and 60 kb, respectively.
source: The EcR binding sites within the E74 and E75 loci have been mapped by ChIP and cover approximately 40 and 60 kb, respectively (Bernardo et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to ChIP mapping study provides supporting evidence.

claim: The heterochromatic band flanking the E75 puff (fragment I) is condensed approximately 25-fold compared to an extended 11 nm chromatin fiber.
source: However, the observed average length of fragment I in living polytene nuclei is only 0.72 (± 0.18) μm, yielding a 25-fold compaction.
evidence: Direct measurement in living cells provides quantitative data.

claim: The heterochromatic band flanking E75 (fragment III) is condensed approximately 22-fold compared to an extended 11 nm chromatin fiber.
source: Similarly, the heterochromatic band (fragment III) flanking E75 appears to be condensed ~22-fold, compared to an extended 11 nm chromatin fiber.
evidence: Direct measurement in living cells provides quantitative data.

claim: The GFP-EcR marked puff (fragment II) shows only threefold compaction compared to an extended 11 nm chromatin fiber.
source: In contrast, measurement of the GFP-EcR marked puff (fragment II) suggested a compaction of only threefold.
evidence: Direct measurement in living cells provides quantitative data.

claim: The chromatin in heterochromatic fragment I is approximately 30-fold more compacted than that in the GFP-EcR-marked puff when considering apparent volumes.
source: When we considered the polytene chromosome as a cylinder, and included diameter measurements to calculate apparent volumes, the difference in chromatin compaction between puffs and bands became even more pronounced. For example, the chromatin in the heterochromatic fragment I appears to be ~30-fold more compacted than that in the GFP-EcR-marked puff of fragment II.
evidence: Calculation based on volume measurements provides quantitative evidence.

claim: GFP-BRM and GFP-BRM-K804R are expressed at comparable levels in S2 cells.
source: Western blotting established that GFP-BRM and GFP-BRM-K804R were expressed at comparable levels, which were well below that of endogenous BRM (Figure 4A).
evidence: Western blot analysis provides quantitative protein expression data.

claim: Both GFP-BRM and GFP-BRM-K804R associate with the full complement of BRM complex subunits.
source: IPs with antibodies directed against GFP followed by mass spectrometry showed that both GFP-BRM and GFP-BRM-K804R associated with the full complement of BRM complex subunits (Figure 4B).
evidence: Mass spectrometry analysis of immunoprecipitates provides biochemical evidence.

claim: Drosophila contains a complex homologous to mammalian GBAF.
source: Interestingly, we identified a homolog of the mammalian GBAF-specific subunit GLTSCR1/L in the GFP-BRM IPs, suggesting that Drosophila contains a corresponding complex.
evidence: Mass spectrometry identification provides biochemical evidence.

claim: GFP-BRM-K804R displays a punctate distribution pattern in S2 cells, unlike the even distribution of wild-type GFP-BRM.
source: Although wild type (wt) GFP-BRM was distributed evenly throughout the nucleoplasm, GFP-BRM-K804R displayed a punctate pattern.
evidence: Confocal imaging provides direct observational evidence.

claim: The punctate pattern of GFP-BRM-K804R is not affected by 1,6-hexanediol treatment.
source: However, the addition of 1,6-hexanediol did not affect the punctate pattern of GFP-BRM-K804R, indicating that phase separation does not explain the clustering of GFP-BRM-K804R (Figure 4C).
evidence: Treatment with 1,6-hexanediol and imaging provides experimental evidence.

claim: The turnover of GFP-BRM-K804R is approximately two-times slower than that of wild-type GFP-BRM in S2 cells.
source: The turnover of GFP-BRM-K804R was approximately two-times slower than that of GFP-BRM, with a time of half recovery (t1/2) of ~ 1.7 (± 1.3) seconds (s) compared to ~ 0.7 (± 0.4) s for wt BRM.
evidence: FRAP analysis provides quantitative kinetic data.

claim: Cancer-associated mutations in the ATP-binding cleft of human SMARCA4 cause a comparable ~2-fold reduction in FRAP recovery kinetics in diploid cells.
source: Cancer-associated mutations in the ATP-binding cleft of human SMARCA4 caused a comparable ~ 2-fold reduction in FRAP recovery kinetics in diploid cells (Hodges et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to previous study provides comparative evidence.

claim: The catalytically inactive BRM-K804R yields two- to fivefold stronger ChIP signals at (P)BAP target loci than wild-type BRM.
source: The catalytically inactive BRM-K804R yielded two- to fivefold stronger ChIP signals at a variety of functional binding sites than wt BRM (Figure 4F).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR analysis provides quantitative binding data.

claim: Loss of ATP-binding causes chromatin retention and clustering of BRM-K804R.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the loss of ATP-binding causes chromatin retention and clustering of BRM-K804R.
evidence: Multiple experimental observations (FRAP, ChIP, imaging) support this conclusion.

claim: GFP-BRM shows rapid recovery after photobleaching of half a nucleus, which is largely complete after approximately 2 minutes.
source: Following photobleaching of half a nucleus, we observed a rapid recovery that was largely complete after ~2 min (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: FLIP-FRAP analysis provides kinetic data.

claim: mCh-H2B shows no recovery within a timeframe of minutes after photobleaching.
source: In contrast to GFP-BRM, mCh-H2B showed no recovery within a timeframe of minutes (min; Figure 5C and D).
evidence: FLIP-FRAP analysis provides kinetic data.

claim: (P)BAP can move freely through the nucleus, whereas the turnover of bulk histones is limited.
source: Thus, (P)BAP can move freely through the nucleus, whereas the turnover of bulk histones is limited.
evidence: FLIP-FRAP results support this conclusion.

claim: GFP-BRM on chromosomes shows a recovery half-time of 3.1 (±1.1) seconds with no substantial immobile fraction.
source: Kinetic analysis revealed a recovery t1/2 of 3.1 (±1.1) s and no substantial immobile fraction.
evidence: FRAP analysis provides quantitative kinetic data.

claim: Co-localization with RNAPII does not substantially affect the FRAP kinetics of GFP-BRM.
source: Finally, co-localization with RNAPII did not affect the FRAP kinetics of GFP-BRM substantially (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: FRAP analysis in different contexts provides comparative data.

claim: The interactions of (P)BAP with chromatin are highly dynamic, with retention times of just a few seconds.
source: The rapid exchange and absence of an immobile fraction shows that the interactions of (P)BAP with chromatin are highly dynamic, with retention times of just a few seconds.
evidence: FRAP kinetic analysis supports this conclusion.

claim: (P)BAP kinetics are dominated by free diffusion in the nucleoplasm.
source: Consequently, (P)BAP kinetics are dominated by free diffusion in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: FRAP results showing rapid exchange and no immobile fraction support this inference.

claim: Photobleaching of chromatin-associated GFP-RPB3 results in an initial rapid increase in fluorescence, followed by a second, more prolonged linear phase of recovery lasting several minutes.
source: In agreement with earlier studies (Yao et al., 2007), photobleaching of chromatin associated GFP-RPB3 resulted in an initial rapid increase in fluorescence, followed by a second, more prolonged linear phase of recovery which lasted for several min (Figure 5G).
evidence: FRAP analysis and citation to previous study provide kinetic data.

claim: The rapid recovery phase of GFP-RPB3 reflects dynamic binding to the promoter, whereas the linear phase corresponds to elongating RNAPII.
source: The rapid recovery at the start probably reflects dynamic binding to the promoter, whereas the linear phase corresponds to elongating RNAPII.
evidence: Interpretation of FRAP kinetics based on known RNAPII behavior.

claim: The turnover of bulk histone H2B is more than two orders of magnitude slower than that of (P)BAP.
source: The turnover of bulk histone H2B is more than two orders of magnitude slower than that of (P)BAP.
evidence: Comparison of FRAP kinetics provides quantitative evidence.

claim: FRAP analysis of GFP-H2B in polytene chromosomes shows it takes over 40 minutes to obtain approximately 20% recovery.
source: FRAP analysis of GFP-H2B in polytene chromosomes revealed that it takes over 40 min to obtain a ~20% recovery (Figure 5H).
evidence: FRAP analysis provides quantitative kinetic data.

claim: Addition of Ec leads to increased RNAPII occupation of the E74 and E75 loci, which peaks approximately 35 minutes after hormone addition.
source: The addition of Ec leads to increased RNAPII occupation of the E74 and E75 loci (monitored by GFP-RPB2), which peaks ~35 min after hormone addition (Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Live-cell imaging and quantification provide temporal data.

claim: FRAP analysis of GFP-RPB2 at the peak of RNAPII accumulation reveals only partial (~60%) recovery that ceases after approximately 5 minutes.
source: FRAP analysis of GFP-RPB2 at the peak of RNAPII accumulation (30 min), revealed only a partial (~60%) recovery that ceased after ~5 min (Figure 6E).
evidence: FRAP analysis provides quantitative kinetic data.

claim: mCh-EcR shows a recovery half-time of 3.0 (±1.1) seconds, comparable to BRM.
source: FRAP analysis of mCh-EcR revealed a recovery t1/2 of 3.0 (± 1.1) s, which is comparable to BRM.
evidence: FRAP analysis provides quantitative kinetic data.

claim: A small but consistent fraction of about 0.14 (±0.07) of mCh-EcR appears to be immobile.
source: In contrast to BRM, however, a small but consistent fraction of about 0.14 (± 0.07) of mCh-EcR appeared to be immobile (Figure 6F).
evidence: FRAP analysis provides quantitative data on mobile fractions.

claim: Histones at the E74 and E75 puffs do not exchange notably.
source: Histones at the E74 and E75 puffs did not exchange notably (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: FRAP analysis provides kinetic data.

claim: GFP-BRD7 co-localizes with mCh-EcR on the E74 and E75 loci, whereas GFP-D4 does not.
source: In agreement with our results for endogenous BAP versus PBAP on fixated polytene spreads (Figure 2D), GFP-BRD7 co-localized with mCh-EcR on the E74 and E75 loci, whereas GFP-D4 did not (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Live-cell imaging provides direct observational evidence.

claim: GFP-BRD7 displays fast FRAP kinetics on the active E74 and E75 loci, comparable to that of BRM.
source: FRAP analysis of GFP-BRD7 revealed fast kinetics on the active E74 and E75 loci, which was comparable to that of BRM (Figure 6H).
evidence: FRAP analysis provides comparative kinetic data.

claim: At the peak of induction, a substantial portion of RNAPII is recycled at the E74 and E75 puffs.
source: In summary, our FRAP results suggest that at the peak of induction, a substantial portion of RNAPII is recycled at the E74 and E75 puffs.
evidence: FRAP analysis and interpretation based on incomplete recovery support this conclusion.

claim: PBAP exchanges rapidly without a substantial immobile fraction at the E74 and E75 loci.
source: However, PBAP, which is essential for expression of E74 and E75, exchanges rapidly without a substantial immobile fraction.
evidence: FRAP analysis provides kinetic data.

claim: (P)BAP acts through a continuous and rapid probing of the genome.
source: We conclude that (P)BAP acts through a continuous and rapid probing of the genome.
evidence: Multiple FRAP experiments showing rapid exchange support this conclusion.

claim: The bulk turnover of histones is limited and slow compared to (P)BAP.
source: By comparison, the bulk turnover of histones is limited and slow.
evidence: FRAP comparison between histones and (P)BAP provides evidence.

claim: Treatment of cultured salivary glands with 0.01% digitonin results in complete loss of NLS-GFP.
source: Treatment of cultured salivary glands with 0.01% digitonin resulted in a complete loss of GFP fused to a nuclear localization signal (NLS-GFP), whereas mCh-H2B remained bound to the chromosomes (Figure 7A).
evidence: Live-cell imaging after permeabilization provides direct observational evidence.

claim: Chromatin-binding of GFP-BRM increases dramatically following permeabilization with digitonin.
source: In striking contrast, chromatin-binding of GFP-BRM increased dramatically following permeabilization.
evidence: Live-cell imaging after permeabilization provides direct observational evidence.

claim: Free GFP-BRM is no longer detectable in the nucleoplasm after permeabilization.
source: Moreover, free GFP-BRM was no longer detectable in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: Live-cell imaging after permeabilization provides direct observational evidence.

claim: Chromatin association of GFP-PC and mCh-RBP3 is substantially reduced in permeabilized glands.
source: Conversely, chromatin association of GFP-PC and mCh-RBP3 was substantially reduced in permeabilized glands.
evidence: Live-cell imaging after permeabilization provides comparative observational evidence.

claim: Chromatin-bound GFP-BRM in permeabilized cells is essentially immobile.
source: Chromatin-bound GFP-BRM in permeabilized cells was essentially immobile, as determined by FRAP (Figure 7C).
evidence: FRAP analysis provides kinetic data.

claim: Following permeabilization, GFP-BRM remains bound to chromatin for more than an hour.
source: Following permeabilization, GFP-BRM remained bound for more than an hour.
evidence: Time-course observation provides temporal data.

claim: Upon addition of ATP, GFP-BRM is immediately released from chromatin and diffuses out of nuclei in permeabilized cells.
source: Tellingly, upon the addition of ATP (2 mM), GFP-BRM was immediately released from chromatin and diffused out of the nuclei (Figure 7D).
evidence: Live-cell imaging after ATP addition provides direct observational evidence.

claim: ATP cannot be replaced by ADP for GFP-BRM release from chromatin.
source: First, ATP could not be replaced by ADP.
evidence: Nucleotide substitution experiment provides functional evidence.

claim: Efficient release of GFP-BRM requires ATP concentrations above 1 mM.
source: Second, efficient release of GFP-BRM required ATP concentrations above 1 mM.
evidence: Dose-response experiment provides quantitative functional evidence.

claim: Neither ATP-γ-S nor ADP-AlF4- can replace ATP for GFP-BRM release.
source: Third, neither the slowly hydrolyzed analogue ATP-γ-S nor the non-hydrolysable ATP ground state mimetic ADP-AlF4- could replace ATP.
evidence: ATP analog substitution experiments provide functional evidence.

claim: The release of GFP-BRM from polytene chromosomes requires hydrolysable ATP at concentrations greater than 1 mM.
source: Thus, the release of GFP-BRM from polytene chromosomes requires hydrolysable ATP at concentrations greater than 1 mM.
evidence: Multiple nucleotide experiments support this conclusion.

claim: Endogenous MOR accumulates on chromatin in permeabilized glands but dissociates and diffuses out of the nucleus upon addition of ATP.
source: Similar to our vital imaging results, we found that MOR accumulated on chromatin in permeabilized glands but dissociated and diffused out of the nucleus upon addition of ATP (Figure 7F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence after permeabilization and ATP treatment provides evidence.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is required for (P)BAP release, but not for binding to chromatin.
source: Taken together, these results show that ATP hydrolysis is required for (P)BAP release, but not for binding to chromatin.
evidence: Permeabilization and ATP addition experiments support this conclusion.

claim: GFP-BRM-K804R co-localizes with endogenous MOR on polytene chromosome spreads.
source: IF of polytene chromosome spreads revealed co-localization of GFP-BRM-K804R with endogenous MOR (SMARCC1/2), indicating largely normal targeting of this mutant (Figure 8A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence provides direct observational evidence.

claim: Chromosomes in GFP-BRM-K804R expressing glands are considerably thinner than in wild-type glands and have an increased tendency to break during preparation.
source: The chromosomes in GFP-BRM-K804R expressing glands, however, were considerably thinner than in wt glands, and had an increased tendency to break during preparation.
evidence: Microscopic observation provides morphological evidence.

claim: Expression of GFP-BRM-K804R leads to DNA under-replication and fragile polytene chromosomes.
source: These observations suggest that the expression of GFP-BRM-K804R leads to DNA under-replication and fragile polytene chromosomes.
evidence: Morphological observations support this inference.

claim: The majority of GFP-BRM-K804R is bound to chromatin in intact salivary glands.
source: Vital imaging of intact salivary glands revealed that, in contrast to wt BRM, the majority of GFP-BRM-K804R is bound to chromatin (Figure 8B).
evidence: Live-cell imaging provides direct observational evidence.

claim: GFP-BRM-K804R has no substantial turnover as shown by FRAP analysis.
source: Moreover, FRAP analysis showed that GFP-BRM-K804R has no substantial turnover (Figure 8C).
evidence: FRAP analysis provides kinetic data.

claim: Permeabilization with digitonin does not affect the chromosome-association of GFP-BRM-K804R in either the presence or absence of ATP.
source: Permeabilization with digitonin, either in the presence or absence of ATP, did not affect the chromosome-association of GFP-BRM-K804R (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: Permeabilization experiments provide functional evidence.

claim: Expression of GFP-BRM-K804R forces binding of endogenous (P)BAP to polytene chromosomes.
source: IF of SNR1 (SMARCB1) showed that the expression of GFP-BRM-K804R forces binding of endogenous (P)BAP to polytene chromosomes (Figure 8F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence provides direct observational evidence.

claim: The addition of 1,6-hexanediol does not affect the diffuse distribution of GFP-BRM nor the clustered binding to interband chromatin of GFP-BRM-K804R.
source: The addition of 1,6-hexanediol, however, affected neither the diffuse distribution of GFP-BRM nor the clustered binding to interband chromatin of GFP-BRM-K804R (Figure 8G).
evidence: Treatment with 1,6-hexanediol and imaging provides experimental evidence.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol reduces the accumulation of mCh-HP1 on the chromocenter.
source: As reported (Strom et al., 2017), 1,6-hexanediol did reduce the accumulation of mCh-HP1 on the chromocenter.
evidence: Treatment experiment and citation provide evidence.

claim: Phase separation does not play a major role in the clustering of GFP-BRM-K804R.
source: The insensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol and the lack of mobility revealed by FRAP suggest that phase separation does not play a major role in the clustering of GFP-BRM-K804R.
evidence: 1,6-hexanediol treatment and FRAP results support this conclusion.

claim: Inadequate release from chromatin drives the local accumulation of BRM-K804R.
source: Rather, we propose that inadequate release from chromatin drives the local accumulation of BRM-K804R (and that of wt BRM in the absence of ATP; see Figure 7).
evidence: Multiple experimental observations support this proposed mechanism.

claim: When co-expressed in larval salivary glands, mCh-BRM-K804R alters the intranuclear distribution of GFP-BRM dramatically, causing it to co-localize with mCh-BRM-K804R on chromosomes.
source: When co-expressed in the larval salivary glands, mCh-BRM-K804R altered the intra nuclear distribution of GFP-BRM dramatically. Instead of being ~95% nucleoplasmic, GFP-BRM now co-localizes with mCh-BRM-K804R on the chromosomes (compare Figures 1I and 8H).
evidence: Live-cell imaging of co-expressed proteins provides direct observational evidence.

claim: In the presence of mCh-BRM-K804R, GFP-BRM becomes immobile as shown by FRAP analysis.
source: Moreover, FRAP analysis showed that in the presence of mCh-BRM-K804R, GFP-BRM also became immobile (Figure 8I).
evidence: FRAP analysis provides kinetic data.

claim: BRM-K804R captures wild-type (P)BAP onto polytene chromosomes.
source: Nevertheless, BRM-K804R captures wt (P)BAP onto polytene chromosomes, possibly via a chromatin-mediated interaction.
evidence: Co-expression and FRAP experiments support this conclusion.

claim: Remodeling may involve direct cooperation or a hand-off mechanism between different BRM complexes.
source: These results raise the intriguing possibility that remodeling involves direct cooperation, or a hand-off mechanism between different BRM complexes.
evidence: Observation that BRM-K804R traps wild-type BRM supports this speculation.

claim: The fluorescence recovery of mCh-H2B overlapping with GFP-BRM-K804R (7±3%) is significantly slower than in the presence of GFP-BRM (18±3%).
source: The fluorescence recovery of mCh-H2B overlapping with GFP-BRM-K804R (7 (± 3) %) was significantly slower than in the presence of GFP-BRM (18 (± 3) %; Figure 8K).
evidence: FRAP analysis provides quantitative comparative data.

claim: Chromatin remodeling and remodeler release are intrinsically coupled.
source: These results suggest that chromatin remodeling and remodeler release are intrinsically coupled.
evidence: Observation that BRM-K804R impedes histone turnover supports this conclusion.

claim: ATP-hydrolysis couples remodeling to SWI/SNF release from chromatin.
source: In vivo analysis reveals that ATP-hydrolysis couples remodeling to SWI/SNF release from chromatin
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the title, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: ATP-hydrolysis drives a continuous transient probing of the genome by (P)BAP.
source: Thus, ATP hydrolysis couples nucleosome remodeling to remodeler release, driving a continuous transient probing of the genome.
evidence: Multiple FRAP and permeabilization experiments support this conclusion.

claim: Loss of ATP hydrolysis enhances chromatin retention and clustering of BRM.
source: Intriguingly, loss of ATP hydrolysis enhanced chromatin retention and clustering of BRM, which was associated with reduced histone turnover.
evidence: Experiments with BRM-K804R mutant provide evidence.

claim: Chromatin condensation excludes (P)BAP, thereby reducing its genomic search space.
source: Based on these observations, we postulate that chromatin condensation excludes (P)BAP, thereby reducing its genomic search space.
evidence: Observations of BRM distribution relative to chromatin condensation support this postulate.

claim: At the height of E74 and E75 transcription, a substantial portion of RNAPII is retained locally in a transcription compartment.
source: At the height of E74 and E75 transcription, a substantial portion of RNAPII is retained locally in what Lis and colleagues named a transcription compartment (Yao et al., 2007).
evidence: FRAP results and citation to previous study support this claim.

claim: PBAP is not retained within a transcription compartment at E74 and E75 loci.
source: On the same chromatin puffs, however, PBAP exchanges rapidly (within ~2–4 s) without a substantial immobile fraction. Thus, although essential for expression of E74 and E75, PBAP is not retained within a transcription compartment.
evidence: FRAP analysis provides kinetic data supporting this conclusion.

claim: Transient binding to chromatin might explain the relatively poor capture of remodelers by ChIP.
source: The rapid exchange of (P)BAP indicates continuous cycles of nucleosome remodeling. Transient binding to chromatin might explain the relatively poor capture of remodelers by ChIP, as the crosslinking reaction has temporal constraints (Gelbart et al., 2005; Schmiedeberg et al., 2009).
evidence: FRAP kinetics and citations to previous studies support this inference.

claim: A mutation in the ATP-binding pocket increased the residence time on chromatin and concomitantly enhanced ChIP signals of BRM-K804R.
source: Indeed, a mutation in the ATP-binding pocket increased the residence time on chromatin and concomitantly enhanced ChIP signals of BRM-K804R.
evidence: FRAP and ChIP experiments provide supporting evidence.

claim: Histone eviction is restricted to small regulatory regions of the genome and is associated with the placement of variant histones.
source: These results agree with the notion that histone eviction is restricted to small regulatory regions of the genome and is associated with the placement of variant histones (Brahma and Henikoff, 2020; Cakiroglu et al., 2019; Deal et al., 2010; Pillidge and Bray, 2019).
evidence: Histone FRAP results and citations to previous studies support this claim.

claim: The prevalent outcome of chromatin remodeling in vivo is restructuring or sliding of nucleosomes rather than eviction.
source: These observations suggest that the prevalent outcome of chromatin remodeling in vivo is restructuring or sliding of nucleosomes rather than eviction.
evidence: Multiple observations about limited histone turnover support this inference.

claim: The level of gray band condensation measured by live-cell imaging agrees well with the value derived from HiC analysis of diploid Kc167 cells.
source: The level of gray band condensation measured by live-cell imaging agrees well with the value derived from HiC analysis of diploid Kc167 cells (Eagen et al., 2015), whereas our imaging-based estimate for black chromatin condensation is ~5-fold higher.
evidence: Comparison with published HiC data provides validation.

claim: Euchromatin and heterochromatin are formed by the same basic nucleosomal array, but at different degrees of condensation.
source: Collectively, these studies suggest that euchromatin and heterochromatin are formed by the same basic nucleosomal array, but at different degrees of condensation.
evidence: Multiple studies including current measurements support this conclusion.

claim: In the absence of ATP hydrolysis, slow release combined with rapid re-binding to a paired chromatid might result in local trapping of (P)BAP on polytene chromosomes.
source: We speculate that in the absence of ATP hydrolysis, slow release combined with rapid re-binding to a paired chromatid, might results in the local trapping of (P)BAP on polytene chromosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed clustering.

claim: Under normal physiological conditions, ATP concentrations in cells would not become depleted to a level (<1 mM) that would impair remodeler function.
source: We note that under normal physiological conditions, ATP concentrations in cells would not become depleted to a level (< 1 mM) that would impair remodeler function.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of cellular ATP levels.

claim: Chromatin binding by BRM is independent of ATP.
source: In contrast, our results with BRM showed that chromatin binding is independent of ATP, but that its release is stimulated by ATP-hydrolysis.
evidence: Permeabilization experiments provide direct evidence.

claim: BRM release from chromatin is stimulated by ATP-hydrolysis.
source: In contrast, our results with BRM showed that chromatin binding is independent of ATP, but that its release is stimulated by ATP-hydrolysis.
evidence: Permeabilization and ATP addition experiments provide direct evidence.

claim: Transient remodeler dynamics enables competition at regulatory elements between epigenetic regulators with opposing effects on chromatin structure.
